power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Given this absence of a standard, we treated the choice as an empirical question: rather than adopting any single published value, we tested four candidates spanning the full range in use (50%, 40%, 30%, and 20% missing data tolerated), recomputing the full exclusion cascade under each, since lowering the coverage requirement also changes the population entering the per-participant baseline z-score calculation, not only the final trial count. The Target mean level in the 1000-1500 ms window was nearly identical across all four candidates (Figure 3B). Because each candidate reduces to a single value per participant, and pupil-size measures are known to be sensitive to outliers (Steinhauer et al., 2022), we compared the four candidates pairwise using sign-flip permutation tests rather than a parametric alternative. Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for the four candidates overlapped substantially (Figure 3B), and none of the six pairwise permutation comparisons was significant, confirming no systematic bias from the choice of threshold within this range. Extending the range to 10-80% (Supplementary Figure S1) showed that only the most stringent value, 10%, which retained less than half of all trials (49.1%), yielded a Target mean level distinguishable from the others (0.073 mm; all pairwise p ≤ .035), whereas 60-80% remained indistinguishable from the literatureanchored range (all p ≥ .28). Given the absence of any detectable difference, a stricter threshold might seem preferable on the grounds that it is more conservative; however, we retained the most permissive value (50%) instead, for a reason grounded in the population rather than in the absence of a measured effect alone. Elevated blink rate in MCI (D'Antonio et al., 2021; Ladas et al., 2014) is a general physiological trait of the participant, largely independent of trial content, rather than a signal-dependent artifact; the stability of the resulting time-course across this entire range is consistent with, though not direct proof of, missingness in this population that is unrelated to the measured response, at least within the range tested. Under these conditions, retaining trials with more missing data does not bias the estimate; it only affects its precision, since data missing completely at random reduce statistical power without distorting the underlying parameter (Little et al., 2012).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Cognitive pupillometry guidelines have been developed and validated almost exclusively on young, healthy participants recorded at high sampling rates, leaving open whether their preprocessing and statistical defaults transfer to harder recording contexts.

Older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) illustrate this problem directly: senile miosis, elevated blink rates, and pharmacologically induced pupillary constriction depart from the assumptions existing pipelines were built on.
Lower-cost, lower-sampling-rate eye trackers, a translationally important target for scalable clinical screening, compound this further.

Using a pooled sample of 67 older adults with MCI from two independent cohorts, recorded at 33 Hz during a visual oddball task, we adapt and empirically justify, decision by decision, a cognitive-pupillometry pipeline for this harder context, evaluating each decision against the well-established Target versus Distractor effect.
Some literature defaults held up unchanged once tested directly against this dataset; others did not transfer; and others had no applicable default at all and were derived empirically.

The Target versus Distractor effect was recovered consistently across every preprocessing alternative tested and across complementary statistical approaches, generalized additive and linear mixedeffects models and trial-level features, whose choice we show depends on whether the question concerns the timing, the average size, or specific components of the effect.

This paper's contribution is not a new pipeline or a clinical marker, but a transparent, reproducible account of which standard assumptions and defaults hold in a harder recording context, which require empirical re-derivation, and which have no existing literature anchor at all, illustrated with accompanying code.

Pupillometry, the measurement of pupil size to study cognitive and emotional processes, is a wellestablished tool in psychology and neuroscience (Beatty & Lucero-Wagoner, 2000; Mathôt, 2018), with applications spanning attention, working memory, arousal, mental effort, and emotion (Bradley et al., 2008; Joshi & Gold, 2020).
text.formatted: Pupillometry, the measurement of pupil size to study cognitive and emotional processes, is a wellestablished tool in psychology and neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beatty & Lucero-Wagoner, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mathôt, 2018)</ref>, with applications spanning attention, working memory, arousal, mental effort, and emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bradley et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Joshi & Gold, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this widespread use, there is no single agreedupon methodology for designing, preprocessing, and analyzing cognitive pupillometry experiments, which limits comparability across studies and complicates replication and metaanalytic synthesis of findings.

In response, comprehensive guidelines have been proposed, most notably by Kret and Sjak-Shie (2019) and Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023) for cognitive pupillometry, complemented by expert consensus standards for pupillography more broadly (Kelbsch et al., 2019), covering experimental design, preprocessing, and statistical analysis, and substantially improving transparency and reproducibility in the field.
text.formatted: In response, comprehensive guidelines have been proposed, most notably by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kret and Sjak-Shie (2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023)</ref> for cognitive pupillometry, complemented by expert consensus standards for pupillography more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kelbsch et al., 2019)</ref>, covering experimental design, preprocessing, and statistical analysis, and substantially improving transparency and reproducibility in the field.

text.text: These guidelines, however, were largely developed and validated on young, cognitively healthy participants tested under controlled laboratory conditions, and whether the same preprocessing defaults generalize to noisier, less well-behaved signals remains untested.
Older adults with cognitive decline, such as those with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), illustrate this problem directly.
Aging alone is associated with a well-documented, luminance-dependent reduction in pupil diameter, called senile miosis (Kelbsch et al., 2019; Winn et al., 1994).
text.formatted: Aging alone is associated with a well-documented, luminance-dependent reduction in pupil diameter, called senile miosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kelbsch et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Winn et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: This brings baseline pupil sizes in this population closer to the 2 mm threshold conventionally used as the lower bound of the "normal" pupillometric range.
This 2 mm threshold is not a hard physiological floor, particularly in MCI.

Pharmacological treatments common in this population can reduce pupil size further: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, the standard pharmacological treatment for MCI and Alzheimer's disease, increase cholinergic tone at the iris sphincter (Nuzzi et al., 2020), and opioids, frequent in pain management in this age group, can constrict the pupil well below 2 mm (Larson, 2008).
text.formatted: Pharmacological treatments common in this population can reduce pupil size further: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, the standard pharmacological treatment for MCI and Alzheimer's disease, increase cholinergic tone at the iris sphincter <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Nuzzi et al., 2020)</ref>, and opioids, frequent in pain management in this age group, can constrict the pupil well below 2 mm <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Larson, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: MCI further adds elevated spontaneous blink rates (D'Antonio et al., 2021; Ladas et al., 2014), and aging a higher prevalence of dry eye (Sharma & Hindman, 2014), which itself shortens the interval between blinks (Johnston et al., 2013); both increase missing or unreliable samples, so preprocessing defaults developed on young, healthy samples cannot simply be assumed to transfer to this population.
text.formatted: MCI further adds elevated spontaneous blink rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(D'Antonio et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Ladas et al., 2014)</ref>, and aging a higher prevalence of dry eye <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sharma & Hindman, 2014)</ref>, which itself shortens the interval between blinks <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Johnston et al., 2013)</ref>; both increase missing or unreliable samples, so preprocessing defaults developed on young, healthy samples cannot simply be assumed to transfer to this population.

text.text: These physiological departures from the standard pupillometric profile are compounded by a second, independent source of difficulty: the recording technology itself.

In recent years, interest in pupillometry and eye tracking as tools for characterizing cognitive decline in MCI and dementia has grown substantially, driven by an explicit translational goal: moving these measures out of specialized laboratories and into scalable, accessible clinical screening tools (Verón et al., 2026; Wolf et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In recent years, interest in pupillometry and eye tracking as tools for characterizing cognitive decline in MCI and dementia has grown substantially, driven by an explicit translational goal: moving these measures out of specialized laboratories and into scalable, accessible clinical screening tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Verón et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wolf et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This goal runs into a concrete practical obstacle.

The infrared eye trackers most commonly used in research to develop and validate cognitive pupillometry pipelines, such as EyeLink systems or the Tobii Pro Fusion, are expensive and require dedicated laboratory infrastructure, which by itself excludes most clinical settings from adopting them at scale.

Low-cost eye trackers, such as those in Tobii's entry-level range, are considerably more feasible for broad clinical deployment (Cuve et al., 2022; Romeo et al., 2024), but do not provide research-grade timing or accuracy: the device used here samples at 33 Hz with an accuracy of approximately 0.65° (Housholder et al., 2022), against EyeLink's typical 1000 Hz sampling and 0.25-0.50° accuracy.
text.formatted: Low-cost eye trackers, such as those in Tobii's entry-level range, are considerably more feasible for broad clinical deployment <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cuve et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Romeo et al., 2024)</ref>, but do not provide research-grade timing or accuracy: the device used here samples at 33 Hz with an accuracy of approximately 0.65° <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Housholder et al., 2022)</ref>, against EyeLink's typical 1000 Hz sampling and 0.25-0.50° accuracy.

text.text: This raises an important methodological question.

Do standard preprocessing and analysis pipelines, developed and validated almost exclusively at higher sampling rates, remain valid once applied to the coarser, noisier signal that lower-frequency, lower-accuracy recording produces?

Because cognitively driven pupil dynamics are slow, with most of their power below approximately 4 Hz (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023), a lower sampling rate need not by itself prevent the response from being captured; the open question is rather whether preprocessing parameters defined in samples or tuned on high-frequency recordings, such as artifact-edge windows, gap limits, and smoothing kernels, transfer to it.

text.text: Prior work using the same attention paradigm adopted here reported an altered target-specific pupil response in MCI and Alzheimer's disease patients compared to healthy controls, peaking progressively later from controls to MCI to Alzheimer's disease and reaching its largest amplitude in Alzheimer's disease (Jiménez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Prior work using the same attention paradigm adopted here reported an altered target-specific pupil response in MCI and Alzheimer's disease patients compared to healthy controls, peaking progressively later from controls to MCI to Alzheimer's disease and reaching its largest amplitude in Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Jiménez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Similar alterations have been reported with other paradigms applied to this population, such as working memory span tasks (El Haj et al., 2022; Granholm et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similar alterations have been reported with other paradigms applied to this population, such as working memory span tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(El Haj et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Granholm et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Like most of the field, these studies did not report or justify their underlying preprocessing decisions in detail.

The present study addresses both gaps in this population and recording context: the lack of a standardized, comparable pupillometry methodology, and the lack of detailed, empirically justified preprocessing decisions in prior pupillometry work with older adults with MCI.
Using a pooled sample of 67 older adults with MCI from two independent cohorts, we recorded pupil responses with the same low-cost eye tracker described above during a visual attention task.
Because such trackers are the practical route toward scalable clinical screening, their output must be held to the same preprocessing rigor as research-grade systems.

We therefore adapt and empirically justify, decision by decision, a cognitive pupillometry pipeline for this population and recording context, extending the same logic from preprocessing to the statistical models applied to the resulting signal, since the simplifying assumptions these models make about the form of the effect over time are themselves untested here.

Existing guidelines, principally Kret and Sjak-Shie (2019) and Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023), provide the starting point: where no applicable default exists, we derive and justify thresholds directly from this dataset, reporting transparently which decisions are literature-anchored and which are dataset-specific.

text.text: Our aim is methodological rather than diagnostic, asking whether the expected pupil responses can be reliably recovered within an MCI population once every preprocessing and analytic decision is made explicit and justified.
Data reported here were drawn from two studies conducted by our research group.

The first (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026b , 2026c) was a cross-sectional study examining the association between the task-evoked pupil response and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease pathology, approved by the Ethics Committees of the University of Barcelona (HCB/2021/0668) and Hospital del Mar.
text.formatted: The first <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Martínez-Flores et al., 2026b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">, 2026c)</ref> was a cross-sectional study examining the association between the task-evoked pupil response and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease pathology, approved by the Ethics Committees of the University of Barcelona (HCB/2021/0668) and Hospital del Mar.

text.text: The second (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a) was a longitudinal study examining the effects of an oculomotor training intervention on oculomotor metrics, including the task-evoked pupil response, and plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration, approved by the Ethics Committee of Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (PR257/24) and prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06963879).
text.formatted: The second <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a)</ref> was a longitudinal study examining the effects of an oculomotor training intervention on oculomotor metrics, including the task-evoked pupil response, and plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration, approved by the Ethics Committee of Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (PR257/24) and prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06963879).

text.text: Both studies were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants, directly or through a legally authorized representative, prior to enrollment.

The pooled sample comprised 67 older adults with a clinical diagnosis of MCI, drawn from the two cohorts described above, collected at different points in time using the same recording device and paradigm.

The first cohort (n = 38, cross-sectional study) was recruited at two clinics in Barcelona, Spain (Hospital del Mar and Hospital Clínic de Barcelona) (age 72.9 ± 5.83 years; 12 men [31.6%], 26 women [68.4%]; MMSE 22.4 ± 4.04).
Other biomarker data beyond pupil size were also collected in this cohort; these are outside the scope of the present study and are reported elsewhere (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026b , 2026c).
text.formatted: Other biomarker data beyond pupil size were also collected in this cohort; these are outside the scope of the present study and are reported elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Martínez-Flores et al., 2026b</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">, 2026c)</ref>.

text.text: The second cohort (n = 29, longitudinal study) was recruited from two residential care facilities under shared administration (Barcelona, Spain).

Of the 30 individuals initially screened, one was excluded prior to baseline assessment due to a medical condition unrelated to the study, yielding a final sample of 29 participants (age 77.5 ± 8.59 years; 13 men [44.8%], 16 women [55.2%]; MoCA 16.2 ± 5.45).

Only the baseline, pre-intervention data from this cohort are used here; the intervention, its outcomes, and the associated plasma biomarker data are outside the scope of the present methodological work and are reported elsewhere (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a).
text.formatted: Only the baseline, pre-intervention data from this cohort are used here; the intervention, its outcomes, and the associated plasma biomarker data are outside the scope of the present methodological work and are reported elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: Across both cohorts, all participants had received a clinical MCI diagnosis from their treating physicians, in accordance with core clinical criteria (Albert et al., 2011; Petersen, 2004).
text.formatted: Across both cohorts, all participants had received a clinical MCI diagnosis from their treating physicians, in accordance with core clinical criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Albert et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Petersen, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Eligibility additionally required participants to be aged 65 years or older, to have sufficient visual function (corrected or uncorrected) to discriminate on-screen stimuli, and to be able to provide informed consent.

Participants were excluded for severe cognitive impairment as judged by the treating physician, a neurological condition resulting in cognitive deficits other than MCI, a major psychiatric diagnosis, structural brain lesions judged to be a primary contributor to cognitive deficits, ophthalmological pathology precluding reliable task performance, or insufficient proficiency in Spanish.
The two cohorts used different cognitive screening instruments (MMSE and MoCA, respectively) and were collected under separate protocols without a shared diagnostic staging framework.

Because of this, and because no healthy control group was collected alongside either cohort, the two samples were pooled exclusively for the methodological validation described here, and no clinical group comparison is attempted.
Both cohorts completed the same visual attention task (Figure 1), following the protocol described by Jiménez et al. (2021).
text.formatted: Both cohorts completed the same visual attention task (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), following the protocol described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Jiménez et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Visual stimuli were presented using the BGaze system (Braingaze SL, Mataró, Spain).
Testing took place in a dimly lit room with curtains drawn and overhead lights off, so that the display screen was the dominant source of ambient illumination throughout each session.
The same recording equipment was used across both cohorts.

Participants were seated approximately 50 cm from the display screen, with a remote binocular eye tracker (Tobii 5L, Tobii Technology AB, Sweden) positioned below it; a chinrest was used throughout to minimize head movement, and corrective lenses were permitted.
Binocular eye position and pupil diameter were recorded continuously at 33 Hz.
The eye tracker was calibrated using a standard five-point binocular procedure before each session.
The task consisted of 120 trials presented in pseudorandom order.

Each trial began with a 2000 ms grey mask screen, followed by a centrally presented stimulus displayed for 2000 ms: an 11-character string of randomly selected upper-or lower-case alphanumeric characters, constructed to avoid meaningful words or acronyms (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Each trial began with a 2000 ms grey mask screen, followed by a centrally presented stimulus displayed for 2000 ms: an 11-character string of randomly selected upper-or lower-case alphanumeric characters, constructed to avoid meaningful words or acronyms (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Stimuli were identical in all physical properties except color: 80% were presented in blue font (distractors) and 20% in red font (targets), with the two colors isoluminant by design, following the Hillyard principle of holding low-level stimulus properties constant between conditions so that only the cognitive state of interest varies (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023).

text.text: Participants were instructed to fixate the screen and press a response button only upon detecting a red string; the experimenter repeated this instruction verbally between trials, when necessary, without interrupting the recording window.
Total task duration was approximately six minutes per session.

Throughout this paper, each preprocessing and analysis decision is evaluated against the within-subject Target-versus-Distractor contrast, a well-established oddball effect that serves as a known benchmark: an appropriate choice should preserve it.

The same procedures apply equally to between-group comparisons, the more common question in this population, which the present data do not support because the two cohorts were not harmonized (Section 5.1).
This question has, however, been addressed with the same approach within each cohort, in relation to biomarker levels and dementia risk (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a , 2026b , 2026c).

Strings shown here are illustrative examples; stimulus order was pseudorandomized across the 120 trials of the task.

We use the term preprocessing to refer to every step that transforms the raw, sample-bysample pupil-size recording given by the eye tracking SDK software into a format suitable for statistical analysis.
This included identifying and excluding invalid samples and trials, reconstructing missing samples, correcting for pre-stimulus fluctuations in pupil size, and smoothing.
As in Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023), the order of these steps is not arbitrary, and we present them here broadly in the order in which they were applied.
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023)</ref>, the order of these steps is not arbitrary, and we present them here broadly in the order in which they were applied.

text.text: General logic and terminology of pupil-size preprocessing are covered in detail elsewhere (Kret & Sjak-Shie, 2019; Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023).
text.formatted: General logic and terminology of pupil-size preprocessing are covered in detail elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kret & Sjak-Shie, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For each step we focus specifically on whether, and why, the recording context of the present study, older adults with MCI, recorded at 33 Hz, required a departure from existing recommendations, and we report the empirical evidence behind each such departure.
Where no departure was necessary, we say so explicitly and adopt the existing recommendation as is.

Cognitive-pupillometry pipelines typically define a physiologically plausible range for raw pupil diameter, since pupil size varies between roughly 2 and 8 mm in diameter under normal conditions (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023).

text.text: This convention, however, was not developed with older or clinical populations in mind, nor validated across the range of consumer-grade devices increasingly used in clinical eye-tracking contexts; absolute pupil-diameter values are not necessarily directly comparable across devices, since device-specific recording and computation methods can shift measurement precision (Romeo et al., 2024).

text.text: Based on this observation, we set the lower bound at 1.5 mm for this population.
We emphasize that this specific value is dataset-specific, and not a general lower bound to be adopted elsewhere.

To further test whether this concentration reflects genuine physiology rather than a tracking artifact, we ran two additional checks: one evaluating interocular concordance directly, the other evaluating whether the decision itself changes the effect this paper reports.

The role of pharmacological treatment specifically is addressed in Section 5.1: in our primary analyses of these cohorts, cholinergic/anticholinergic medication status showed no relevant effect on the pupil response.

If the 1.5-2 mm band reflected corneal-reflection tracking noise rather than true measurement, interocular agreement should be worse in this band than in an equally narrow window elsewhere in the plausible range, since genuine miosis is consensual across the two eyes while tracking noise need not be.
We compared interocular agreement (Bland-Altman) for samples in the 1.5-2.0 mm range (n = 97,653) and samples in the 2.0-2.5 mm range (n = 117,410; Figure 2C).

text.text: Bias and limits of agreement were closely comparable between the two ranges (1.5-2.0 mm: bias = 0.040 mm, 95% LOA = [-0.672, 0.753] mm; 2.0-2.5 mm: bias = 0.075 mm, 95% LOA = [-0.666, 0.815] mm), with the 1.5-2.0 mm range showing marginally tighter, not wider, agreement.
In other words, there is no excess interocular disagreement in the 1.5-2 mm range.

More directly, we tested whether this decision changes the reported effect itself: we re-ran the complete exclusion cascade (minimum coverage, baseline z-score, boundary edge, max gap; see the next sections) using a minimum pupil diameter of 2.0 mm, the conventional default, in place of the production value, and compared the resulting Target time-course mean in the same 1000-1500 ms window used elsewhere in this pipeline (Figure 2D).

text.text: Our chosen lower bound of 1.5 mm yielded a Target window-mean of 0.065 mm (n = 67 participants, BCa 95% CI = [0.044, 0.085]), and conventional lower bound of 2.0 mm yielded 0.056 mm (n = 59, BCa 95% CI = [0.036, 0.078]); a paired permutation test on the 59 participants with data under both floors found no significant difference (mean diff = 0.008 mm, p = .113).
Beyond leaving the reported effect unchanged, the lower bound of 1.5 mm retained eight additional participants who would otherwise have been dropped for insufficient valid data.

Together, these two checks indicate that the 1.5-2 mm band is not distinguishable from the surrounding range on interocular agreement, and that adopting it in place of the conventional 2 mm default does not alter the effect this paper reports, while retaining more usable data.

text.text: Even when a trial retains enough valid data, the two eyes may not be tracked equally well.

Age-related dry eye (see Introduction), together with eyelash occlusion and gaze-dependent measurement error in corneal-reflection eye trackers (Brisson et al., 2013), can leave one eye substantially better tracked than the other within a given trial.

text.text: Averaging both eyes indiscriminately under these conditions introduces noise from the poorer-quality eye rather than genuine binocular signal.

To quantify this imbalance, we computed, for each trial, the coverage of each eye: the percentage of samples in the post-stimulus window that were flagged as valid by the eye tracker, fell within the screen, and lay within the plausible pupil range defined in Section 3.1.1.
We then expressed the two as a ratio, the coverage of the worse-tracked eye divided by that of the bettertracked eye.
A ratio of 1 means both eyes were tracked equally well; a ratio near 0 means one eye contributed almost no valid data.
When the ratio fell below a given threshold, only the better eye's samples were used; otherwise both eyes were averaged, with samples valid in only one eye taken from that eye alone.
Using the better-covered eye when the other has excessive missing data is common practice, but no generally adopted criterion for when to do so exists.

Rather than fixing a value a priori, we plotted, for each candidate threshold, the percentage of trials (among those meeting the minimum coverage criterion, Section 3.1.2) that would be switched to single-eye data, and looked for a region where small changes in the threshold produced negligible changes in this percentage (Figure 3C).

text.text: This stable region spanned ratios of approximately 0.25-0.40, within which about 2.0% of trials were switched, a small percentage, consistent in spirit with Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) ~5% guideline for artifact checks.
We selected 0.30 within this region: both eyes were averaged only if the worse eye covered at least 30% of what the better eye covered.
A closely related decision concerns the maximum single gap within a trial that can reasonably be reconstructed through interpolation rather than left as unreliable.

Reconstruction algorithms in this literature typically impose an upper limit on gap length, on the grounds that interpolation is only meaningful over periods short enough for pupil size to remain predictable.

A gap duration of 500 ms is the threshold conventionally used in the literature to define the maximum plausible duration of a single blink (Steinhauer et al., 2022); Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) blinkreconstruct() algorithm, for example, does not attempt to interpolate gaps longer than 500 ms, whereas Kret and Sjak-Shie (2019) did not interpolate over gaps longer than 250 ms in their worked example, so the literature offers two reference points rather than one.

Because the oddball paradigm used here assigns unequal saliency to Target and Distractor stimuli, an asymmetry that has no counterpart in Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) original design, the exclusion and reconstruction criteria described above could in principle be applied unevenly across conditions, for instance if one condition were associated with systematically more blinking or poorer tracking than the other. text.text: Once a trial's maximum tolerable gap has been established (Section 3.1.4), any gap that survives must be reconstructed before the signal can be baseline-corrected and averaged.

The pupillometry preprocessing literature generally recommends one of two interpolation methods for this purpose: linear interpolation, which draws a straight line between the two valid samples bounding a gap, or cubic-spline interpolation, which fits a smooth curve using additional anchor points on either side.

Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) blinkreconstruct() algorithm, for example, is not neutral between the two: it attempts cubic-spline interpolation first, using two additional anchor points on either side of the gap, and falls back to a straight line only when those additional points are unavailable.
Their stated rationale is that a smooth curve "more closely resembles natural pupil-size changes" than a straight line.

This preference, however, rests on the plausibility of a smooth reconstruction rather than on validation against ground truth, and was developed on highfrequency recordings from young, healthy samples, where gaps are typically brief and anchor points are drawn from a comparatively clean signal.

Elevated spontaneous blink rate in MCI (D' Antonio et al., 2021; Ladas et al., 2014) means gaps are both more frequent and, on average, longer in this population, giving the choice of reconstruction method more opportunity to matter, and making the anchor points cubic-spline interpolation depends on more likely to themselves sit in a noisier stretch of signal.

text.text: To test whether Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) recommendation was appropriate for our data, we compared the two methods in two complementary ways, implementing the same local, four-point cubic-spline procedure their algorithm itself uses (two valid samples immediately before the gap, two immediately after), rather than a spline fit across the whole trial, so that the comparison reflects the actual reconstruction method being evaluated.
First, we compared the two methods directly against each other.

For each trial, we identified the longest stretch of missing data and took the sample at its temporal midpoint, the point furthest from any valid data and therefore where the two reconstructions are free to diverge the most.
We then compared the value reconstructed at that sample by linear and by cubic-spline interpolation, yielding one pair of values per trial.
This comparison was run on the baseline-corrected but unsmoothed signal, to isolate the interpolation method's own contribution from the separately justified smoothing step (Section 3.4).

Across all accepted trials, the two methods correlated strongly (r = .92) but showed a Bland-Altman bias of 0.053 mm and 95% limits of agreement of [-0.39, 0.49] mm at the point of maximal divergence (Figure 4A-B), wide relative to the effect under study, although this represents a worst case at the single-sample level rather than its impact on the averaged response.

text.text: A direct disagreement between two methods, however, only shows that they differ, not which one is more accurate.

To answer that question, we validated both methods against known ground truth using synthetic gap injection: gaps of realistic length, sampled from this dataset's own distribution of real gap lengths, were artificially introduced into trials with otherwise complete raw signal, then reconstructed via both methods and compared against the original, unblanked signal at the gap's midpoint (resampled onto the 33 Hz analysis grid).

Across 3,000 synthetic gaps, linear interpolation was closer to the true value in 70.4% of cases overall (Wilcoxon test on absolute error, p < .001), and its root-mean-square error (RMSE) against ground truth remained essentially flat regardless of gap length (approximately 0.05-0.06 mm throughout).

The baseline period was defined as the last 7 samples (212 ms at 33 Hz) of the preceding mask screen, immediately before stimulus onset. Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023) recommend keeping the baseline period short, both because a short window is less likely to be contaminated by blinks or artifacts, and because, when a baseline period coincides with stimulus onset, its duration must stay below 200 ms to avoid capturing the earliest phase of the pupil light response.

text.text: Because our baseline window falls entirely within the preceding mask and therefore fully precedes stimulus onset, it is not subject to this second constraint; its short duration follows the same general logic of minimizing artifact contamination.

Because mask and stimulus durations were fixed, anticipatory dilation may have contributed to the baseline; since participants could anticipate when, but not whether, a Target would appear, any such effect would apply to both conditions alike.

No evidence in the literature suggests that a different baseline duration is better suited to older adults with MCI, so we retained this minimal, literature-anchored window without empirical re-derivation.
Using this baseline period requires two further decisions: how to summarize the baseline window into a single value per trial, and how to identify and exclude trials with an anomalous baseline.

Both decisions conventionally rely on the mean and standard deviation: the mean as the summary value, and deviation from the participant's mean in units of standard deviation as the exclusion rule, with Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023) recommending the exclusion of trials with |z| > 2.

Once the signal has been reconstructed, a final smoothing step is standard practice in psychophysiological pupillometry (Steinhauer et al., 2022) to reduce residual high-frequency noise before averaging.

text.text: The appropriate smoothing method depends on the sampling rate of the recording and on which component of the signal is of interest: filtering that is appropriate for isolating a fast, high-frequency signal is not necessarily appropriate for a slow one, and vice versa.

Following this logic, we specified six trial-level features to be extracted from the baselinecorrected pupil signal, each intended to capture a different aspect of the response visible in the grand-average waveform: an initial slope (linear regression of pupil size on time, in mm/s, over the first 500 ms), a global slope (the same regression over the full trial duration), a late slope (the same regression restricted to 1000 ms onward, capturing the sustained portion of the response), the area under the curve (trapezoidal integration of pupil size over time, in mm•ms), the time to peak (the time, in ms, at which the absolute baseline-corrected pupil size reaches its maximum), and peak amplitude (that maximum absolute value, in mm).

These features and their windows were specified a priori, following prior studies using this paradigm (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a , 2026b , 2026c), in which they were defined on the grandaverage waveform collapsed across stimulus types, and therefore independently of the Target-Distractor contrast tested here.

text.text: The value of this technique is more likely to be realized in a use case common in this population, comparing a full response curve between separate groups, for instance MCI patients against cognitively healthy older adults, or across different biomarker-defined or clinical stages of impairment, where the shape and timing of any between-group divergence is not known in advance and a predetermined window would risk missing where in the trial the groups actually differ.
Cognitive pupillometry data can be analyzed at different levels of detail, and the appropriate method depends on the question being asked rather than on any single preferred technique.

If the question is how an effect unfolds over time (when it emerges, when it peaks, whether it has distinct phases), the full time-course must be modeled, and a generalized additive mixed model (4.1) does so without assuming its shape.

If the question is how large the effect is on average, a linear mixed-effects model with a single coefficient (4.2) answers it directly and interpretably, and is closely equivalent to analyzing each trial's mean or area under the curve.

Between these two lies the analysis of trial-level features (4.3): by decomposing each trial into a small set of summary values specified a priori, such as the initial slope, time to peak, or peak amplitude, specific aspects of the response's temporal shape can be tested with the same simple models, without the complexity of a GAMM.
These approaches are complementary rather than redundant.

The GAMM describes the whole shape of the response but yields no single effect size for downstream analyses such as correlations with biomarkers or comparisons between groups, whereas the single-coefficient model and trial-level features yield such effect sizes but capture only the aspects of the response specified in advance.
We therefore recommend, when feasible, reporting the full time-course alongside one or more summary measures chosen to match the study's hypothesis (Table 1).
text.formatted: We therefore recommend, when feasible, reporting the full time-course alongside one or more summary measures chosen to match the study's hypothesis (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: These recommendations are not specific to MCI and apply to cognitive pupillometry in general.

They weigh more heavily, however, in samples like the present one, where unequal trial counts between conditions, data quality that varies widely between participants, and strong autocorrelation at a low sampling rate make the assumptions behind model-based inference harder to take for granted.
In the present Target-versus-Distractor comparison, we therefore proceed from the most to the least detailed description of the effect.

A generalized additive mixed model (4.1) models the non-linear time-course of each condition and the autocorrelation between samples directly, and shows how the difference between conditions unfolds: it becomes reliable at approximately 485 ms and grows to a maximum of 0.118 mm at approximately 1455 ms.

A linear mixed-effects model with a single coefficient (4.2) then summarizes this difference as its average across the trial; although it uses every sample, it is in practice a summary-value analysis, closely related to the trial-level features specified in Section 3.6 and analyzed in Section 4.3, such as the area under the curve or the global slope.

Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) cross-validation technique addresses the same underlying question by a different route: it uses part of the data to locate the sample at which the difference between conditions, or groups, is largest, and tests the difference at that sample in the held-out data.

It is therefore equally applicable to within-subject and between-group comparisons, and in many cases answers the same question as a GAMM; we use the GAMM here because it additionally describes the shape of the difference across the whole trial.

Most pupillometry studies that test an effect against the full time-course of the pupil response do so either by extracting a small number of features per trial (peak amplitude, latency, mean pupil size within a window) or by fitting mixed-effects models with polynomial time terms to the trajectory (van Rij et al., 2019).

The pupil dilation response to a salient stimulus is a smooth, asymmetric curve, and assuming a fixed functional form without checking the actual shape of the signal risks both under-fitting genuine non-linear structure and mis-specifying the autocorrelation of the model residuals, which itself inflates Type I error (van Rij et al., 2019).

text.text: Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) address both problems from within the same model, rather than treating them as separate corrections layered on afterward.

A smooth term for time, allowed to take a different shape for each condition, lets the curve differ between Target and Distractor trials rather than only its overall level; an additional smooth term for time nested within participant absorbs each individual's own non-linear trajectory, the additive-model equivalent of the "keep it maximal" logic for random effects (Barr et al., 2013) applied to curve shape rather than to a single slope.
text.formatted: A smooth term for time, allowed to take a different shape for each condition, lets the curve differ between Target and Distractor trials rather than only its overall level; an additional smooth term for time nested within participant absorbs each individual's own non-linear trajectory, the additive-model equivalent of the "keep it maximal" logic for random effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref> applied to curve shape rather than to a single slope.

text.text: Critically, GAMMs also allow a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) correlation structure to be estimated and fit directly into the model, letting the model itself, rather than a separate correction applied to the test statistic, account for the dependency between neighboring samples that motivates Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) multiple-comparisons techniques in the first place.
We modeled baseline-corrected pupil size with stimulus (Target vs.
Distractor) as the predictor of interest.

Rather than assuming any particular shape over time, the model estimated a smooth curve over time for each condition, so that Target and Distractor could differ not only in their overall level but also in the shape of their time-course.

A second smooth curve was estimated for each participant, allowing each participant's response to take its own shape, in the same spirit as a by-participant random slope in a linear mixed model (Baayen et al., 2017).

text.text: Because consecutive pupil samples are strongly correlated, the model must also account for this autocorrelation; otherwise it treats every sample as independent information and overstates the certainty of its estimates (van Rij et al., 2019).

text.text: We did this in two steps.
We first fit the model without any correction and measured how strongly each residual correlated with the next one within the same trial, never across trial boundaries.
This correlation was nearly perfect (ρ = .986).
We then refit the model with a first-order autoregressive, or AR(1), term fixed at that value, which tells the model that each sample largely repeats the information of the one before it.
The correction barely changed how well the model fit the data (deviance explained 16.69% vs.

16.37%), but the estimated curves became more flexible (effective degrees of freedom, a measure of how 'wiggly' a curve is, where 1 corresponds to a straight line, increased from about 9.5 to about 15 for each condition).
We report the AR(1)-corrected model (Table 2).

text.text: To characterize when within the trial window this divergence emerges, we additionally computed the population-level difference curve (Target minus Distractor), excluding the by-participant smooth, with a 95% confidence band derived from the model's full coefficient covariance matrix, which properly propagates parameter uncertainty rather than naively combining two separate per-condition standard errors.

The confidence interval excluded zero at 51 of the 67 unique timepoints sampled across the trial window, from approximately 485 ms onward to the end of the window; the difference peaked at 0.118 mm (95% CI [0.110, 0.125]) at approximately 1455 ms, consistent with a divergence that emerges early and is sustained for most of the window rather than being confined to a brief interval.

This approach is most valuable whenever the question concerns how an effect unfolds over time, or whether the relationship with a continuous predictor is linear: it models the shape of the signal rather than assuming it, and accounts for temporal autocorrelation within the model itself.

When the question is instead the average size of an effect across the trial, a linear mixed-effects model offers a substantially simpler and more directly interpretable estimate (4.2), and the two approaches agree on that average, as shown next.

The generalized additive model described above shows how an effect unfolds over time, but it comes at a real cost in complexity and interpretability: a single, directly interpretable effect size is harder to extract from a set of smooth terms than from a single regression coefficient (Wood, 2017).

text.text: The two resampling procedures answer distinct questions.

A block-permutation test addresses whether the effect exists at all: the stimulus label of each trial is shuffled within participant, which leaves each trial's samples, and therefore their autocorrelation, intact, and the model is refit on each relabeled dataset.
Because the autocorrelation is preserved in every permuted dataset, it affects the null distribution exactly as it affects the observed statistic, so the resulting pvalue remains valid.

Because the observed labeling is itself one of the possible permutations, a permutation p-value is bounded below by 1/(B + 1), where B is the number of permutations, and can never be exactly zero (Phipson & Smyth, 2010); results beyond this bound are therefore reported as p < .001.

To verify that the block-permutation test keeps its nominal false-positive rate when samples are this strongly autocorrelated, we additionally ran a calibration check by simulation: we generated 100 datasets with no stimulus effect by construction (15 participants, 20 trials each with 20%

A well-calibrated test should return p < .05 in approximately 5% of these datasets, with p-values uniformly distributed.

This agreement confirms that the simpler model recovers the average effect correctly, while the GAMM additionally shows how that difference evolves over time.

text.text: In populations that are inherently difficult to measure, such as older adults with MCI, data quality varies widely between participants, and some retain relatively few trials after qualitycontrol exclusions; in the oddball paradigm used here, the 20% Target frequency further reduces the number of Target trials per participant.

A mixed-effects model already accounts for unequal tested against it, one change at a time relative to the production pipeline: neither the choice of minimum pupil diameter, baseline criterion, smoothing filter, nor coverage threshold changed the qualitative outcome, even where the specific numerical estimate shifted, and the interpolation method retained was the more accurate of the two against ground truth.

This robustness could not have been established without the decision-by-decision testing reported here: without it, the choice of any single default would have been an untested assumption rather than a confirmed non-issue, and a smaller or subtler effect could easily have depended on exactly the choice that here made no difference.

This pattern is what a decision-by-decision adaptation is meant to produce: not a single correct pipeline, but confidence that the reported effect is a property of the population and paradigm rather than an artifact of any single preprocessing choice among several defensible ones.
This decision-by-decision test produced no uniform verdict on the guidelines it started from, and that absence of a uniform verdict is itself informative.

Some defaults held up unchanged once tested: the 500 ms maximum-gap threshold was corroborated within under one percentage point by a data-driven elbow, and Mathôt's mean-based baseline z-score criterion (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023) agreed with a more robust MAD-based alternative (Leys et al., 2013) on 97.7% of exclusion decisions, and was the more conservative of the two.

text.text: Others did not transfer: cubicspline interpolation, Mathôt and Vilotijević's (2023) stated preference, performed worse than simple linear interpolation against ground truth when implemented as the same four-point local fit their algorithm uses.

Still others had no applicable default at all and were derived empirically from this dataset alone: the minimum pupil-size cutoff, informed by this sample's pupil-size distribution and checked against interocular agreement and its effect on the reported response, rather than the generic 2 mm heuristic; the interocular coverage ratio threshold, anchored to an empirical selection curve; and the minimum per-trial coverage, retained after permutation tests across the full range of literature-anchored cutoffs found no detectable bias.

This pattern, spread across defaults that transfer, defaults that do not, and genuine gaps, suggests that existing cognitive-pupillometry guidelines generalize reasonably across sampling rate and population for some preprocessing stages but not others, consistent with the field's broader lack of a single standardized preprocessing framework (Schwartz et al., 2026).

The statistical analysis adds a complementary point.

The techniques Mathôt and Vilotijević (2023) propose for the multiple-comparisons problem fit a separate model at every sample and therefore make no assumption about the shape of the pupil time-course; summarizing an effect with a single coefficient, by contrast, answers a narrower question, the average size of the effect across the trial, and is silent on how it unfolds.

Both patterns just described, partial transfer of preprocessing defaults and the added necessity of statistical verification in this population, converge on the translational motivation stated in the Introduction: moving cognitive pupillometry out of specialized laboratories and into more accessible clinical and lower-cost recording contexts (Cuve et al., 2022; Romeo et al., 2024; Wolf et al., 2023).

text.text: The guidelines this paper builds on were developed and validated on eye trackers such as EyeLink or Tobii Pro systems, sampling at rates an order of magnitude higher than the 33 Hz used here.

Every threshold that required empirical derivation in this paper rather than direct reuse, the minimum pupil size, interocular coverage balance, and minimum per-trial coverage, was one where the coarser temporal resolution and noisier signal of a lower-cost, lowersampling-rate tracker plausibly changes where a reasonable cutoff falls.

This paper's central practical message for that translational goal is accordingly not that any specific threshold reported here should be copied into a lower-cost pipeline, but that preprocessing itself is a sensitive stage that must be adapted and re-tested for the recording conditions at hand, rather than copied wholesale from pipelines built for laboratory-grade, high-sampling-rate eye trackers.

The pipeline's decisions were tested on two independently collected cohorts, so each threshold and modeling choice was evaluated under more heterogeneous recording conditions than a single cohort would provide.

The resulting sample, 67 participants and close to 600,000 raw samples, was large enough to support the data-driven checks this paper relies on, which would be considerably noisier, or infeasible, in a smaller sample.
Because every check is implemented in the accompanying code, researchers can re-run them on their own data rather than adopt the thresholds reported here.
This work also has limitations.

No healthy older-adult comparison group was available, so we cannot rule out that some empirically derived thresholds would differ in healthy older adults, and all data came from a single session per participant, so their stability across sessions remains untested.

Because screening instrument, biomarker modality, and cohort are confounded in this sample (Section 2.1), neither between-group comparisons nor pooled covariates for medication status and cognitive severity were possible, although neither covariate showed a relevant effect within each cohort (Martínez-Flores et al., 2026a , 2026b , 2026c).

text.text: Finally, a single paradigm, population, and eye tracker were used, so the specific thresholds reported here should be re-derived rather than transferred directly to other contexts.

This paper adapted a cognitive-pupillometry pipeline, decision by decision, to older adults with MCI recorded at 33 Hz, a context that departs substantially from the one existing guidelines were developed on.

Its contribution is not a new method or a clinical marker, but a transparent account of which defaults hold in this harder context, which require empirical re-derivation, and which have no literature anchor at all.

For researchers adapting a pipeline to a new or harder-to-measure population, we summarize the workflow illustrated in this paper as the following recommendations:  Inspect the raw pupil-size distribution and eye coverage before adopting exclusion thresholds, and test whether each choice changes the reported effect, using the same participant-level analysis for every check.
selection curve or a comparable data-driven check before adopting them.

 Compare interpolation methods in matched implementations, validate them against ground truth, for example by synthetic gap injection, and default to the simpler method unless a more complex one performs better.
 Compare baseline criteria on the pre-exclusion sample to avoid circularity, and use robust alternatives, such as a MAD-based criterion, as diagnostic cross-checks rather than silent replacements.
 Disclose when a processing choice, such as the smoothing method, follows prior work, and test whether the data also support it.
 Check known confounds, such as gaze position or eye coverage, for differences between conditions, and report them even when no correction is applied.

 Fix analysis windows and trial-level features independently of the tested contrast, from prior literature or a waveform collapsed across conditions or groups, and use the grand average of that contrast only as a manipulation check.

 Choose the statistical approach according to the question (Table 1): a GAMM to describe how an effect unfolds over time, and a linear mixed-effects model or a priori trial-level features to estimate its size or specific components.

We refit the full time-series LMM from Section 4.2 once per participant (67 refits), each time excluding that participant, using the identical model formula, REML fit, and optimizer settings as the original model.

The Target coefficient ranged from 0.063 to 0.069 mm across the 67 refits (M = 0.066 mm), close to the full-sample estimate of 0.066 mm and never approaching zero or reversing sign, and no refit produced a singular fit or a convergence failure.

No single participant's exclusion moved the estimate by a meaningful margin, indicating that the Target versus Distractor effect reported in Section 4.2 is not being driven by a small subset of participants.

The first is temporal autocorrelation: consecutive samples within the same trial are not independent observations, since pupil diameter changes slowly and smoothly over time, so neighboring time points share far more variance with each other than with samples drawn at random from the same trial.
